stories.title: Gorham Middle School Students Support Sustainability and Dignity with Thrift Shop
stories.summary: Two eighth graders turned a small idea into Rams Rack, a student-run thrift store inside Gorham Middle School offering free clothes and resources. Since opening, over 253 items have found new homes, giving peers both style and dignity.
stories.extended_summary: What started as a brainstorm after volunteering at Maine Needs is now a full-on boutique inside Gorham Middle School. Eighth graders Rataj and Leela pitched their vision for a stigma-free thrift store to school leaders, and then built it from the ground up — cleaning an old library space, collecting donations, even designing a logo with a local artist. Rams Rack has already moved 253+ pieces, giving students access to clothes they need without any shame. "Some love the sustainability, some love the find," but for those who need it, the store provides real dignity. All because two students saw compassion and spread it.

stories.title: Race4Chase helps thousands of children carry on Sandy Hook victim's dream
stories.summary: A mother's promise after losing her son in Sandy Hook has grown into Race4Chase, a triathlon program that has helped over 5,000 kids across the country. It carries on 7-year-old Chase Kowalski's love of the sport, turning tragedy into a wave of young athletes.
stories.extended_summary: After Chase Kowalski was killed in the 2012 Sandy Hook shooting, his mother Rebecca had a vision: "Mama, we're going to change the world." She created Race4Chase, a triathlon training program for children. What started in a few Connecticut YMCAs now operates in dozens of locations nationwide, boasting more than 5,000 kids who've completed a triathlon. Chase's dream, cut short at age seven, now lives on through every young finisher.

stories.title: Roadside milkweed is giving monarchs a new migration highway
stories.summary: Researchers have planted 9,000 milkweed plants along Florida roadways, and monarch butterflies are already showing up. The effort turns everyday highway margins into lifelines for pollinators, with 6,000 more plants planned by 2029.
stories.extended_summary: Monarch butterflies are getting a new highway of their own. In six North Florida counties, researchers have planted 9,000 milkweed plants along roadsides, with thousands more on the way. It's part of a national project to transform managed lands like highway strips and power line easements into usable pollinator habitat. Early results are promising: monarchs are already visiting the plants. Because protected lands alone aren't enough to sustain butterfly populations, this approach could turn everyday infrastructure into a conservation superhighway.

stories.title: Small events that win big gifts, no gala required
stories.summary: Nonprofits are ditching black-tie galas for intimate dinners that connect donors directly to the mission. One couple, moved by a family's story at a small steakhouse event, committed $25,000 before the night ended. This anti-gala approach is winning big gifts on a smaller budget.
stories.extended_summary: In a steakhouse dining room in Austin, about a dozen guests listened as families shared how alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency had reshaped their lives. One couple, briefly connected to the foundation, committed $25,000 that evening. This is the anti-gala: small, private events that put the mission front and center, replacing hard asks with authentic storytelling. Fundraising leaders say the approach deepens relationships and converts newcomers into major donors—often with less time and money than splashy galas. It's proof that sometimes, the most powerful pitch is simply hearing someone's story.

stories.title: The Commercial Street Bridge on the Parkway East Reopens Monday Night
stories.summary: Pittsburgh's Parkway East reopened in under three weeks after crews slid a 22-million-pound bridge into place using an accelerated construction technique. Commuters got relief ahead of schedule, with PennDOT calling the project a stunning achievement.
stories.extended_summary: Nightmare traffic on the Parkway East ended a week early. The Commercial Street Bridge project, originally slated to finish by Aug. 3, opened on July 27 after crews worked around the clock. The secret? An accelerated bridge construction method that laterally slid the 22-million-pound span 102 feet onto the existing alignment. Combined with round-the-clock labor and incentives for early completion, the project finished in less than three weeks. PennDOT secretary Mike Carroll described it simply: "A stunning achievement."

stories.title: This Kentucky Jail Has Grown More Than 41,000 Pounds of Produce
stories.summary: Henderson County Detention Center's garden program has produced over 41,300 pounds of fresh vegetables this year. Inmates learn practical skills, teamwork, and responsibility while growing food that feeds the jail and supports the community.
stories.extended_summary: A county jail that grows more produce than many farms? That's Henderson County Detention Center, where eligible inmates help plant, maintain, and harvest thousands of pounds of vegetables. This year's haul has already passed 41,300 pounds. The program goes beyond feeding the facility—surplus produce goes to local organizations, and inmates gain hands-on experience in teamwork, planning, and safe work practices. There's even a vermicomposting operation. It's a cultivated path toward reentry, one growing season at a time.

stories.title: UMass Amherst professor gets $1.3M grant to develop more accurate at-home HIV test
stories.summary: A UMass Amherst professor received a $1.3M NIH grant to develop a highly accurate at-home HIV test. The test aims to close the global awareness gap, helping millions learn their status and curb transmission.
stories.extended_summary: Today's at-home HIV tests often miss early infections, but a new technology from UMass Amherst could match lab-level accuracy. Engineering professor Chang Liu landed a two-year, $1.3 million NIH grant to push the test toward commercial use. The goal: help close the "first 95" benchmark—ensuring 95% of people living with HIV know their status. Currently, only 87% do worldwide, leaving an estimated 5.3 million unaware. Liu's test could be a game-changer, especially in rural and resource-limited areas where access to clinics is hardest.

stories.title: Why this new affordable condo community in East Austin only has one parking spot
stories.summary: East Austin's Ivory is a carless condo complex with 40 affordable units for families earning up to 70% of median income. By skipping parking, the nonprofit developer created more homes—and turned a parking lot into possibility.
stories.extended_summary: At the corner of Chicon and 14th Street sits a condo building with no parking lot—just one handicap spot. The Ivory is Austin's first carless condominium complex, born from the city's Affordability Unlocked program. In exchange for forgoing parking, the nonprofit developer could add more units, reserving 40 of them for families at 70% of median income. For a two-person household, that's a cap of $75,250. It's a swap that trades asphalt for homes, proving that fewer parking permits can mean more doors open.

stories.title: ‘Kids are actually eating the food’: State expands lunch program that pairs schools with farms
stories.summary: California's Farm to School program turns lunchrooms into fans of fresh food—students beg for pozole refills and a middle-schooler says he's never heard a complaint. The program is now permanent and expanding statewide.
stories.extended_summary: In Lake Tahoe schools, kids line up for rambutan, shout for more pozole, and actually ask staff to refill the salad bar. The secret? California's Farm to School program, which connects districts with local farmers and ranchers. It's been such a hit that the state just made it permanent. Among its fans is one middle-schooler who declared, "I have literally never heard anyone complain about the food." Districts also get grants for farm field trips and kitchen trainings. For educators, it's the end of soggy pizza—and the beginning of students eating their greens, willingly.

stories.title: Barclay Pies Ups the Ante for Gluten-Free Pizzas in Cherry Hill
stories.summary: Barclay Pies in Cherry Hill serves gluten-free pizza so good it's now a third of their orders. They use separate ovens to prevent cross-contamination, making a favorite food safe and delicious for everyone.
stories.extended_summary: At Barclay Pies, gluten-free isn't an afterthought—it's a specialty. Food critic Craig LaBan says the high-hydration crusts, dusted with cornmeal, rival the real thing. The shop bakes its gluten-free pizzas in separate ovens to avoid cross-contamination, even offering gluten-free mozzarella sticks. The result? About one-third of all orders are now gluten-free. For those with celiac or sensitivity, it's a chance to enjoy a Detroit-style slice without worry. The owners' mission: make a truly inclusive pizzeria, and it's paying off one safe, crispy bite at a time.

stories.extended_summary: MADISON — In May, Drew University wrapped up the inaugural semester of its Empty Nester program , designed for adults adjusting to life after their kids move out of the house. The course is open to all adult learners, with a focus on intergenerational learning, says Angelina Brown, long life learning coordinator for the Empty Nester program at Drew. While most students are between the ages of 50 and 65, she says there are some in their 40s, 70s, and 80s. Anyone who is in a life transition will find this program rewarding, Brown said. The goal of the Empty Nester program is for long life learners to seek intellectual engagement, personal enrichment and community connection in midlife and beyond, Brown said. stories.title: First flex homes at Ephraim Crossing available for purchase
stories.summary: Ephraim's first FlexReady homes are now for sale, starting at $369,000—well below the city's $547,000 average. Built to expand from three bedrooms to six, they offer affordable housing that grows with a family.
stories.extended_summary: The Landing at Ephraim Crossing introduces a new take on first homes: houses that can grow with you. The base model costs $369,000 and includes 1,240 square feet, three bedrooms, and 1.5 baths. But thanks to pre-installed plumbing, electrical, and HVAC connections, owners can add a second story, extra bedrooms, or even a rental unit—up to 2,500 square feet and six bedrooms. FlexReady Homes even offers support during the first five years of expansion projects. It's a creative answer to workforce housing, earning the project a Utah First Homes Award.

stories.title: Kosher dining pops up in Jackson Hole for the summer
stories.summary: Jackson Hole, a remote mountain town, just got its first-ever kosher restaurant this summer. Three rabbinical students drove from Brooklyn to make it happen, serving hundreds of meals to visitors from around the world.
stories.extended_summary: Deep in the Wyoming mountains, where celebrities go to escape, there was one thing you couldn't find: freshly prepared kosher food. For 20 years, the only option was Rabbi Mendelsohn's kitchen. So three rabbinical students packed up from Brooklyn and set up the Kosher Jackson Hole Grill, spending nearly 100 hours on logistics before they even opened. By mid-July, they'd dished out hundreds of meals to visitors from over a dozen countries — plus locals who'd never had the option. It's a summer pop-up that's about way more than food: it's a mitzvah, a lifeline, and a reminder that remote doesn't have to mean unreachable.

stories.title: Salt Water, Support Systems Inspire at Surf Therapy Event
stories.summary: Waves of Strength’s Adaptive Surf Therapy Day brought 150 participants with cognitive, developmental and physical challenges to Long Beach Island to ride waves with volunteer support. For many, it was a life-changing experience—one nonverbal boy even started speaking after his surf session.
stories.extended_summary: At Brant Beach, hundreds of volunteers surrounded each surfer in the water, ready to share the stoke. Wave of Strength’s annual event gives kids and young adults with disabilities a chance at the healing power of the ocean. For one 12-year-old, the experience unlocked something amazing: after hearing him stay silent his whole life, his father heard him speak for weeks. Founder Rob Simek started the event eight years ago with 20 participants; now it draws 150 surfers and over 200 volunteers.

stories.title: THE BREAKFAST KLUB: Houston’s HBCU Send Off Is A Vibe
stories.summary: Marcus and Mel Davis shut down The Breakfast Klub’s parking lot each year to throw a massive send-off party for Houston students heading to HBCUs. With free food, DJs, games and scholarship money, the event helps freshmen build community before college starts.
stories.extended_summary: In downtown Houston, a parking lot turns into the ultimate HBCU celebration. The Breakfast Klub’s annual Freshmen Send-Off Party welcomes over 100 incoming college students with snow cones, dancing, giveaways and real scholarships. No parents allowed inside—just future classmates bonding before they leave home. Founder Marcus Davis, a Texas Southern alum, wants students to see other people who look like them thriving in these spaces, so they start their journey with a built-in network.

stories.title: Tahoe’s bears can get too comfortable with humans. These dogs help bring back healthy fear
stories.summary: Nevada wildlife officials use Karelian Bear Dogs Badger and Banjo to haze bears that get too comfortable around people. The goal is to restore bears' natural fear of humans, reducing conflicts while helping the recovering bear population coexist with Tahoe communities.
stories.extended_summary: Badger and Banjo wear fur coats year-round and take no salary—but they’re crucial members of Nevada’s bear team. The Karelian Bear Dogs chase and nip at bears that have become too used to human food, teaching them to avoid people. They also flush bears from urban dens and help rescue injured ones. Wildlife biologists say the dogs are key to keeping Tahoe’s bears wild, even as the region fills with humans.

stories.title: The Communities We’ve Built in Prison
stories.summary: At a Tennessee prison, a writing club helped 78-year-old Dave, who never learned to read or write, compose a letter to his daughter—and hear back. Their support has reunited a dozen men with their families. The effort is a reminder of the power of community.
stories.extended_summary: One evening, 78-year-old Dave rolled his wheelchair up to a writing club table in prison and asked for help writing a letter to his daughter. He’d been incarcerated for 40 years and never learned to read or write. Decades ago, a letter he sent got returned, and he gave up. Club members wrote with him, he got a reply, and now his daughter visits with his three grandkids. The club has since helped over a dozen prisoners reconnect with their families.
